The functions Φk​R​LK,Φk​R​LJ\Phi_{kRL}^{K},\Phi_{kRL}^{J} are the linear combinations of the solutions ϕR​L​(𝐫R,ϵν​κ​R​l)≡ϕκ​R​L\phi_{RL}({\bf r}_{R},\epsilon_{\nu\kappa Rl})\equiv\phi_{\kappa RL} to the radial Schrödinger equation as well as their energy derivatives ϕ˙R​L​(𝐫R,ϵν​κ​R​l)≡ϕ˙κ​R​L\dot{\phi}_{RL}({\bf r}_{R},\epsilon_{\nu\kappa Rl})\equiv\dot{\phi}_{\kappa RL} taken at the energies ϵν​κ​R​l.\epsilon_{\nu\kappa Rl}. In the interstitial region, the linear MT orbitals are represented as multicenter expansions [left–hand side of Eq. (25)]. In order to calculate the interstitial–potential matrix elements and represent the charge density, we use the Fourier transform of the LMTOs in the interstitial region. It is impossible to consider the Fourier transform of the expression (25) directly because of the singularities in the Hankel functions. On the other hand, since this representation will be used for the description of the basis functions only within Ωi​n​t,\Omega_{int}, we can substitute the divergent part of the Hankel function by a smooth function for rR<sR.r_{R}<s_{R}. This regular function is defined in the Appendix and it is denoted as K~κ​R​L.\tilde{K}_{\kappa RL}. We thus introduce a pseudoLMTO |χ~κ​R​L𝐤⟩|\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}\rangle defined in all space as follows:

χ~κ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫)\displaystyle\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r}) =\displaystyle= ∑tei​𝐤𝐭​K~κ​L​(𝐫R−𝐭)=\displaystyle\sum_{t}e^{i{\bf kt}}\tilde{K}_{\kappa L}({\bf r}_{R}-{\bf t})= (27)
=\displaystyle= ∑Gχ~κ​R​L​(𝐤+𝐆)​ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)​𝐫,\displaystyle\sum_{G}\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}({\bf k}+{\bf G})e^{i({\bf k}+{\bf G}){\bf r}},

which is identical with the true sum (25) in the interstitial region.

The charge density and the potential have a dual representation: spherical-harmonic expansions inside the MT-spheres and plane-wave expansions in the interstitial region. This is usually done by introducing a smooth pseudocharge density ρ~\tilde{\rho} in all space defined in terms of the pseudoLMTOs (27). The pseudodensity coincides with the true density when 𝐫∈Ωi​n​t.{\bf r}\in\Omega_{int}.\,In this way, the solution of the Poisson equation is straightforward and can be done along the lines developed in Ref. 34. In practical applications we have also used the technique described in the Appendix for the Fourier transform of the Coulomb interactions and for the construction of auxiliary densities. The exchange–correlation potential is found using the fast Fourier transform and the interstitial–potential matrix elements are explicitly evaluated.

b. Changes in the linear muffin-tin orbitals.

We shall now discuss the linear–response calculation. Small displacements of atoms from their equilibrium positions defined by expression (1) lead to the change in the Bloch sum of the atom–centered (pseudo) Hankel functions (27). Because of the explicit dependence of the basis functions |χκ​R​L𝐤⟩|\chi_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}\rangle on the atomic positions 𝐑{\bf R}, here and in the following the displaced atoms will be denoted by the index 𝐑¯.{\bf\bar{R}.} The change in the Bloch sum of the MT orbitals can be found analogously to the change in the external potential in Eqs.(2)–(4). As a result, we consider two travelling waves with wave vectors 𝐤+𝐪{\bf k}+{\bf q} and 𝐤−𝐪{\bf k}-{\bf q}, i.e.

δ±​χ~κ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫)δ​R¯μ=−δR¯​R∑tei⁡(𝐤±𝐪)​𝐭∇μK~κ​R​L(𝐫R−𝐭)=\displaystyle\frac{\delta^{\pm}\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}=-\delta_{\bar{R}R}\sum_{t}e^{i({\bf k}\pm{\bf q}){\bf t}}\nabla_{\mu}\tilde{K}_{\kappa RL}({\bf r}_{R}-{\bf t})=
−δR¯​R∑Gi(k±q+G)μ×χ~κ​R​L(𝐤±𝐪+𝐆)ei⁡(𝐤±𝐪+𝐆)​𝐫,\displaystyle-\delta_{\bar{R}R}\sum_{G}i(k\pm q+G)_{\mu}\times\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}({\bf k}\pm{\bf q}+{\bf G})e^{i({\bf k}\pm{\bf q}+{\bf G}){\bf r}},
(28)

which represent the change of the basis functions in the interstitial region or the change of the pseudoLMTOs in the whole space. Here we have restored the original notations: δ±​χ~κ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫)/δ​R¯μ≡δ±​χ~κ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫)\delta^{\pm}\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r})/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}\equiv\delta^{\pm}\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r}). We also introduce a spherical coordinate system [33]:

𝐑¯=∑μR¯μ​eμ=R¯−1​e−1+R¯0​e0+R¯+1​e+1,{\bf\bar{R}=}\sum_{\mu}\bar{R}_{\mu}e^{\mu}=\bar{R}_{-1}e^{-1}+\bar{R}_{0}e^{0}+\bar{R}_{+1}e^{+1}, (29)

which is connected to the Cartesian system as follows: R¯−1=+(R¯x−iR¯y)/2,R¯0=R¯z,R¯+1=−(R¯x+iR¯y)/2.\bar{R}_{-1}=+(\bar{R}_{x}-i\bar{R}_{y})/\sqrt{2},\bar{R}_{0}=\bar{R}_{z},\bar{R}_{+1}=-(\bar{R}_{x}+i\bar{R}_{y})/\sqrt{2}. The reason is that, in the spherical coordinates, the operation ∇μ\nabla_{\mu} on a product of a radial function f⁡(r)f(r) multiplied by the spherical harmonic takes the simple form:

∇μf​(r)​Yl​m​(𝐫)=\displaystyle\nabla_{\mu}f(r)Y_{lm}({\bf r})=
4​π3​Cl​m​l+1​m+μ1​μ​(d​fd​r−lr​f​(r))​Yl+1​m+μ​(𝐫)+\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{3}}C_{lml+1m+\mu}^{1\mu}\left(\frac{df}{dr}-\frac{l}{r}f(r)\right)Y_{l+1m+\mu}({\bf r})+
4​π3​Cl​m​l−1​m+μ1​μ​(d​fd​r+l+1r​f​(r))​Yl−1​m+μ​(𝐫).\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{3}}C_{lml-1m+\mu}^{1\mu}\left(\frac{df}{dr}+\frac{l+1}{r}f(r)\right)Y_{l-1m+\mu}({\bf r}). (30)

We shall now find variation of the basis functions inside the MT spheres. In the sphere 𝐑′{\bf R}^{\prime}, the original LMTO is defined in the expression (26). Its change must include both the changes in the numerical radial functions and the change in the structure constants:

δ±​χκ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫R′)δ​R¯μ=δ±​Φκ​R​LK​(𝐫R)δ​R¯μ​δR′​R−\displaystyle\frac{\delta^{\pm}\chi_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r}_{R^{\prime}})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}=\frac{\delta^{\pm}\Phi_{\kappa RL}^{K}({\bf r}_{R})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}\delta_{R^{\prime}R}-
∑L′δ±​Φκ​R′​L′J​(𝐫R′)δ​R¯μ​γR′​l′​SR′​L′​R​L𝐤​(κ)−\displaystyle\sum_{L^{\prime}}\frac{\delta^{\pm}\Phi_{\kappa R^{\prime}L^{\prime}}^{J}({\bf r}_{R^{\prime}})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}\gamma_{R^{\prime}l^{\prime}}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)-
∑L′Φκ​R′​L′J​(𝐫R′)​γR′​l′​δ±​SR′​L′​R​L𝐤​(κ)δ​R¯μ.\displaystyle\sum_{L^{\prime}}\Phi_{\kappa R^{\prime}L^{\prime}}^{J}({\bf r}_{R^{\prime}})\gamma_{R^{\prime}l^{\prime}}\frac{\delta^{\pm}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}. (31)

The change in the numerical functions contains two contributions. Since Φκ​R​LK\Phi_{\kappa RL}^{K}, Φκ​R​LJ\Phi_{\kappa RL}^{J} are constructed from the solutions of the radial Schrödinger equation and their energy derivatives, ϕκ​R​L\phi_{\kappa RL} and ϕ˙κ​R​L,\dot{\phi}_{\kappa RL}, the change in ϕκ​R​L\phi_{\kappa RL} and ϕ˙κ​R​L\dot{\phi}_{\kappa RL} is a result of both the rigid movement of the spherical component of the potential and the change in the shape of the spherical component. In the following, it is convenient to treat the rigid movements of the potential within the MT–sphere centered at 𝐑{\bf R} separately, i.e. represent the total change in the form:

δ±​Ve​f​f​(𝐫R)δ​R¯μ=−δR¯​R​∇μVe​f​f​(𝐫R)+δ(s)±​Ve​f​f​(𝐫R)δ​R¯μ,\frac{\delta^{\pm}V_{eff}({\bf r}_{R})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}=-\delta_{\bar{R}R}\nabla_{\mu}V_{eff}({\bf r}_{R})+\frac{\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}V_{eff}({\bf r}_{R})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}, (32)

where the notation δ(s)±\delta_{(s)}^{\pm} stands for the ”soft” change, i.e. the variation connected with the change in the shape of the function. The functions δ±​ϕκ​R​L/δ​R¯μ\delta^{\pm}\phi_{\kappa RL}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} are represented in a form similar to (32), i.e. δ±​ϕκ​R​L/δ​R¯μ=−δR¯​R​∇μϕκ​R​L+δ(s)±​ϕκ​R​L/δ​R¯μ\delta^{\pm}\phi_{\kappa RL}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}=-\delta_{\bar{R}R}\nabla_{\mu}\phi_{\kappa RL}+\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\phi_{\kappa RL}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}, where the last (soft) contribution is found by solving the radial Sternheimer equation:

(−∇r2+l⁡(l+1)r2+Ve​f​fS​P​H−ϵν​κ​R​l)​δ(s)±​ϕκ​R​Lδ​R¯μ+\displaystyle(-\nabla_{r}^{2}+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^{2}}+V_{eff}^{SPH}-\epsilon_{\nu\kappa Rl})\frac{\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\phi_{\kappa RL}}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}+
(δ(s)±​Ve​f​fS​P​Hδ​R¯μ−δ(s)±​ϵν​κ​R​lδ​R¯μ)​ϕκ​R​L=0.\displaystyle\left(\frac{\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}V_{eff}^{SPH}}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}-\frac{\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\epsilon_{\nu\kappa Rl}}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}\right)\phi_{\kappa RL}=0. (33)

The superscript ”S​P​HSPH” here denotes the spherical component of the potential and the perturbation. It is, in principle, not a problem to take all non–spherical terms of the perturbation into account. If this is done, the first–order changes in the radial functions are no longer given by a single spherical harmonic but as an expansion in Yl​mY_{lm}. One obtains an uncoupled system of radial equations, which can easily be solved [10]. However, in the problem of lattice dynamics the change in ϕκ​R​L\phi_{\kappa RL} and ϕ˙κ​R​L\dot{\phi}_{\kappa RL} due to the change in the shape of the spherical component of the potential is small. This is because the motions of atoms mainly distort the dipole part of the potential. If the change in the shape of the spherical component can be described by some constant shift of the energy, it may be cancelled by appropriate choice of the change δ(s)±​ϵν​κ​R​l/δ​R¯μ\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\epsilon_{\nu\kappa Rl}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} in the energies ϵν​κ​R​l.\epsilon_{\nu\kappa Rl}. This cancellation can, for instance, be obtained by finding δ(s)±​ϵν​κ​R​l/δ​R¯μ\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\epsilon_{\nu\kappa Rl}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} with fixed logarithmic derivatives Dν​κ​R​lD_{\nu\kappa Rl} . (The derivatives Dν​κ​R​lD_{\nu\kappa Rl} are evaluated at the occupied centers of gravities of the bands for the unperturbed crystal.) We thus see that the influence of the constant shifts to the change in the basis set can be eliminated and, therefore, one can neglect by the contribution δ(s)±​ϕκ​R​L/δ​R¯μ\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\phi_{\kappa RL}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} in practical calculations. The accuracy of this approximation is quite good which has already been confirmed by good agreement between total energy and force calculations with the original LMTO method[26] where the same approximation was used for deriving the force formula.

We now give the formula for the change in the structure constants which enters Eq. (31). It is expressed as the difference between the gradients of the structure constants for wave vectors 𝐤{\bf k} and 𝐤±𝐪,{\bf k}\pm{\bf q,} i.e

δ±​SR′​L′​R​L𝐤​(κ)δ​R¯μ=\displaystyle\frac{\delta^{\pm}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}=
δR¯​R′​∇μSR′​L′​R​L𝐤​(κ)−δR¯​R​∇μSR′​L′​R​L𝐤±𝐪​(κ).\displaystyle\delta_{\bar{R}R^{\prime}}\nabla_{\mu}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)-\delta_{\bar{R}R}\nabla_{\mu}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}}(\kappa). (34)

The gradient is with respect to 𝐑′−𝐑{\bf R}^{\prime}-{\bf R}. From (30), using the recursion relations for the Hankel functions, it follows that the change in the structure constants can be expressed in terms of the structure constants:

∇μSR′​l′​m′​R​l​m𝐤​(κ)=\displaystyle\nabla_{\mu}S_{R^{\prime}l^{\prime}m^{\prime}Rlm}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)=
=i\displaystyle\ =i 4​π3​Cl′−1​m′−μ​l′​m′1​μ​κ2​sR′(2​l′−1)​SR′​l′−1​m′−μ​R​l​m𝐤​(κ)+\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{3}}C_{l^{\prime}-1m^{\prime}-\mu l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}^{1\mu}\frac{\kappa^{2}s_{R^{\prime}}}{(2l^{\prime}-1)}S_{R^{\prime}l^{\prime}-1m^{\prime}-\mu Rlm}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)+
+i\displaystyle+i 4​π3​Cl′+1​m′−μ​l′​m′1​μ​(2​l′+1)sR′​SR′​l′+1​m′−μ​R​l​m𝐤​(κ).\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{3}}C_{l^{\prime}+1m^{\prime}-\mu l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}^{1\mu}\frac{(2l^{\prime}+1)}{s_{R^{\prime}}}S_{R^{\prime}l^{\prime}+1m^{\prime}-\mu Rlm}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa). (35)

Here, the left index of the structure constants has changed to l′±1,m′−μl^{\prime}\pm 1,m^{\prime}-\mu, but the right index l​mlm\,remains the same. An analogous formula exist in which the right index change is l±1,m+μl\pm 1,m+\mu in and the left index is unchanged.

It is seen that the change in the MT orbital (31) can be represented as a rigid part, a small soft part and a contribution from the change in the structure constants:

δ±​χκ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫R′)δ​R¯μ\displaystyle\frac{\delta^{\pm}\chi_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r}_{R^{\prime}})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}} =\displaystyle= −δR¯​R′​∇μχκ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫R′)+δ(s)±​χκ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫R′)δ​R¯μ−\displaystyle-\delta_{\bar{R}R^{\prime}}\nabla_{\mu}\chi_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r}_{R^{\prime}})+\frac{\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\chi_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r}_{R^{\prime}})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}- (36)
∑L′Φκ​R′​L′J​(𝐫R′)​γR′​l′​δ±​SR′​L′​R​L𝐤​(κ)δ​R¯μ.\displaystyle\sum_{L^{\prime}}\Phi_{\kappa R^{\prime}L^{\prime}}^{J}({\bf r}_{R^{\prime}})\gamma_{R^{\prime}l^{\prime}}\frac{\delta^{\pm}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}.

It is convenient to separate the rigid part since it gives rise to a rigid contribution in the electronic response:

δ±​ρ​(𝐫R)δ​R¯μ=−δR¯​R​∇μρ​(𝐫R)+δ(s)±​ρ​(𝐫R)δ​R¯μ.\frac{\delta^{\pm}\rho({\bf r}_{R})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}=-\delta_{\bar{R}R}\nabla_{\mu}\rho({\bf r}_{R})+\frac{\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\rho({\bf r}_{R})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}. (37)

Since the induced charge density (37) has the same form as the change in the potential (32), we need not calculate the gradients of the charge density and the potential. This is important since these gradients are huge in the core region, which could result in large numerical errors. The second term in (36) is δ(s)±​χκ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫R′)/δ​R¯μ\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\chi_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r}_{R^{\prime}})/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}. It is constructed from the changes δ(s)±​ϕκ​R​L/δ​R¯μ\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\phi_{\kappa RL}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} and their energy derivatives which are numerically small. This function is exactly equal to zero together with its first-order radial derivative at the sphere sR′s_{R^{\prime}}. It translates like a Bloch wave with vector 𝐤±𝐪{\bf k}\pm{\bf q} because the original form of one–center expansion (26) translates with wave vector 𝐤{\bf k} while the first–order changes δ(s)±​ϕκ​R​L/δ​R¯μ\delta_{(s)}^{\pm}\phi_{\kappa RL}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} translate, like the perturbation, with wave vector ±𝐪\pm{\bf q}. The whole expression (36) also translates with wave vector 𝐤±𝐪{\bf k}\pm{\bf q} and fits into the multicenter expansion of the change in the basis set in the interstitial region [formula (28)]. However, since the original LMTOs are continuous and only differentiable to first order at the boundaries of the MT spheres, the matching of the change in the basis set is only continuous but not differentiable. This, in principle, leads to a kink in the change of the charge density. However, it does not have any effect in the calculation of the dynamical matrix if the latter is compared with the second–order derivative of the total energy derived from the frozen-phonon supercell calculation. This is so because the extension of the LMTO method described here is just an analytical version of the finite-difference approach employed in the supercell technique. When applied to the same problem, the results of both approaches have to be the same except for the errors introduced by taking finite differences. This concerns the comparison of not only the dynamical matrix and the phonon frequencies, but also the changes in the basis set, the expansion coefficients, the charge densities and in all other quantities which can be obtained by the frozen–phonon LMTO technique.

We now turn to the problem of calculating the change in the expansion coefficients Aκ​R​L𝐤​j,A_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}j}, which are necessary to compute the first–order corrections according to (13). From expression (17), the change δ±​Aκ​R​L𝐤​j/δ​R¯μ\delta^{\pm}A_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}j}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} is given by

δ±​Aκ​R​L𝐤​jδ​R¯μ\displaystyle\frac{\delta^{\pm}A_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}j}}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}} =\displaystyle= ∑j′Aκ​R​L𝐤±𝐪​j′ϵ𝐤​j−ϵ𝐤±𝐪​j′\displaystyle\sum_{j^{\prime}}\frac{A_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}}}{\epsilon_{{\bf k}j}-\epsilon_{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}}} (38)
×(δ±​H𝐤±𝐪​j′​𝐤​jδ​R¯μ−ϵ𝐤​j​δ±​O𝐤±𝐪​j′​𝐤​jδ​R¯μ)\displaystyle\times\left(\frac{\delta^{\pm}H^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}{\bf k}j}}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}-\epsilon_{{\bf k}j}\frac{\delta^{\pm}O^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}{\bf k}j}}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}\right)

and it is expressed in terms of the change in the hamiltonian and the overlap matrices. Here, the change in the matrix elements of the hamiltonian is given by the band representation:

δ±​H𝐤±𝐪​j′​𝐤​jδ​R¯μ=∑κ′​R′​L′∑κ​R​LAκ′​R′​L′𝐤±𝐪j′∗δ±​Hκ′​R′​L′​κ​R​Lδ​R¯μAκ​R​L𝐤​j\frac{\delta^{\pm}H^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}{\bf k}j}}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}=\sum_{\kappa^{\prime}R^{\prime}L^{\prime}}\sum_{\kappa RL}A_{\kappa^{\prime}R^{\prime}L^{\prime}}^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}*}\frac{\delta^{\pm}H_{\kappa^{\prime}R^{\prime}L^{\prime}\kappa RL}}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}A_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}j} (39)

and a similar formula holds for the matrix elements of the overlap integral. In the original, {κ​R​L},\{\kappa RL\}, representation the changes δ±​Hκ′​R′​L′​κ​R​L/δ​R¯μ\delta^{\pm}H_{\kappa^{\prime}R^{\prime}L^{\prime}\kappa RL}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} andδ±​Oκ′​R′​L′​κ​R​L/δ​R¯μ\,\delta^{\pm}O_{\kappa^{\prime}R^{\prime}L^{\prime}\kappa RL}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu} are readily computed using the formulae (28) and (36) for the first–order changes in the basis set. It is indeed even more advantageous to find the corresponding formulae by directly varying the expressions for the hamiltonian and the overlap matrices. This avoids the problem of combining the contributions with the gradients of numerical radial functions to the surface integrals. One point about calculating the change in the interstitial kinetic–energy matrix elements and the interstitial overlap integrals is worth noticing. Since these matrix elements contain energy–derivative of the structure constants, the change in these matrix elements will contain the change in this energy derivative. The corresponding formula can be found by taking the derivative with respect to κ2\kappa^{2} in the expressions (34) and (35).

Another problem is to find second–order changes in the LMTO basis functions as well as second–order variations in the Hamiltonian and the overlap matrices. They are necessary for computing the incomplete–basis–set corrections in (11) for the dynamical matrix. In the interstitial region the second–order change in the pseudoLMTOs is simply given by:

δ+​δ−​χκ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫)δ​R¯μ′′​δ​R¯μ\displaystyle\frac{\delta^{+}\delta^{-}\chi_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r})}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu^{\prime}}^{\prime}\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}} =\displaystyle= δR¯′​R​δR¯​R​∑Gi​(k+G)μ′​i​(k+G)μ\displaystyle\delta_{\bar{R}^{\prime}R}\delta_{\bar{R}R}\sum_{G}i(k+G)_{\mu^{\prime}}i(k+G)_{\mu} (40)
×χκ​R​L​(𝐤+𝐆)​ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)​𝐫.\displaystyle\times\chi_{\kappa RL}({\bf k}+{\bf G})e^{i({\bf k}+{\bf G}){\bf r}}.

Inside the MT spheres the expression is more complicated, but can be found straightforwardly by performing one more variation δ−/δ​R¯μ′\delta^{-}/\delta\bar{R}_{\mu^{\prime}} of expression (31) for the first–order change. It will contain second–order changes in the numerical radial functions and second–order changes in the structure constants as well as different products of the first–order changes in these quantities. The second–order changes in the structure constants are given by

δ+​δ−​SR′​L′​R​L𝐤​(κ)δ​R¯μ′′​δ​R¯μ=\displaystyle\frac{\delta^{+}\delta^{-}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu^{\prime}}^{\prime}\delta\bar{R}_{\mu}}=
δR¯​R′​∇μδ−​SR′​L′​R​L𝐤​(κ)δ​R¯μ′′−δR¯​R​∇μδ−​SR′​L′​R​L𝐤+𝐪​(κ)δ​R¯μ′′.\displaystyle\ \delta_{\bar{R}R^{\prime}}\nabla_{\mu}\frac{\delta^{-}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}}(\kappa)}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu^{\prime}}^{\prime}}-\delta_{\bar{R}R}\nabla_{\mu}\frac{\delta^{-}S_{R^{\prime}L^{\prime}RL}^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}}(\kappa)}{\delta\bar{R}_{\mu^{\prime}}^{\prime}}. (41)

This is obtained from the expression (34) and δ−​S𝐤\delta^{-}S^{{\bf k}} is expressed via the difference between the gradients of the structure constants for the wave vectors 𝐤{\bf k}\, and 𝐤−𝐪{\bf k}-{\bf q}, while δ−​S𝐤+𝐪\delta^{-}S^{{\bf k}+{\bf q}} is the difference between ∇S\nabla S\, for the wave vectors 𝐤+𝐪{\bf k}+{\bf q}\, and 𝐤.{\bf k.} Alternatively, the expression (41) can be found by first considering the expression for the structure constants in the supercell and then, assuming the form (1) for the atomic displacements, transferring the supercell expression to the original structure. The second–order gradients ∇μ′∇μ​S\nabla_{\mu^{\prime}}\nabla_{\mu}\,S are calculated using (35) and they are again the structure constants with the left index changed to l′±2,m′−μ′−μl^{\prime}\pm 2,m^{\prime}-\mu^{\prime}-\mu and unchanged right index. Analogously, they can be expressed in terms of the structure constants of the same left index l′​m′l^{\prime}m^{\prime} and the right index: l±2,m+μ′+μ.l\pm 2,m+\mu^{\prime}+\mu.

The second–order changes in the numerical radial functions must also be calculated. They contain contributions ∇μ′∇μ​Φκ​R​LK,J\nabla_{\mu^{\prime}}\nabla_{\mu}\Phi_{\kappa RL}^{K,J} due to the rigid movement of the spherical part of the potential to second order, changes due to the rigid movements of the first–order variations in the shape of the spherical part (rigid movement of the soft part), as well as the contributions arising from the change in the shape of the spherical part to second order (second–order soft part). As we discussed above, one can neglect by the influence of the change in the shape of Ve​f​fS​P​HV_{eff}^{SPH} to the change in the basis. Therefore, we must only keep the rigid contributions described by ∇μ′∇μ​Φκ​R​LK,J.\nabla_{\mu^{\prime}}\nabla_{\mu}\Phi_{\kappa RL}^{K,J}.

c. Brillouin-zone integrals.

After computing the first–order corrections to the wave functions, we have to perform the 𝐤{\bf k}-space integration over the first Brillouin zone (BZ) in order to find the change in the charge density from Eq. (6). The BZ integration is also required for calculating the incomplete-basis-set corrections to the dynamical matrix. It is in general a full–zone integration while for the high–symmetry wave vectors the integrals are reduced to that portion of the BZ which is irreducible with respect to the symmetry of the perturbation vector.

Two kinds of the integrals have to be performed in the linear–response calculation. The first one has the following form

I1​(𝐪)=∑𝐤​j2​f𝐤​j​Ak​j​(𝐪)I_{1}({\bf q})=\sum_{{\bf k}j}2f_{{\bf k}j}A_{kj}({\bf q}) (42)

and the second one is given by

I2​(𝐪)=∑𝐤​j​j′2​f𝐤​j​(1−f𝐤±𝐪​j′)ϵ𝐤​j−ϵ𝐤±𝐪​j′​M𝐤±𝐪​j′​𝐤​j.I_{2}({\bf q})=\sum_{{\bf k}jj^{\prime}}\frac{2f_{{\bf k}j}(1-f_{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}})}{\epsilon_{{\bf k}j}-\epsilon_{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}}}M^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}{\bf k}j}. (43)

where Ak​j​(𝐪)A_{kj}({\bf q}) and M𝐤±𝐪​j′​𝐤​jM^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}{\bf k}j} are the matrix elements which presumably are smooth functions of wave vectors. In order to calculate these integrals we use the tetrahedron method in Ref. 35. In this method, the BZ is set up by the reciprocal–lattice translational vectors and it is divided into small primitive cells exactly as in standard fast–Fourier–transform analysis. The calculation becomes simpler if the 𝐪{\bf q} vector coincides with a mesh point because 𝐤±𝐪{\bf k}\pm{\bf q} vectors are also mesh points. In this way the energy bands, the expansion coefficients, and the structure constants have to be calculated only once at the mesh of the irreducible wave vectors 𝐤{\bf k} for the unperturbed crystal. Applying symmetry operations, these quantities can be found for any general 𝐤{\bf k}.

When applied to a semiconductor, the tetrahedron method is identical to the special–point method of Monkhorst and Pack[37], which means that the occupation numbers f𝐤​jf_{{\bf k}j} in (42) and (43) can be regarded as the geometrical weights of the 𝐤{\bf k}–points. Both integrals (42) and (43) converge rapidly with respect to the number of 𝐤{\bf k}–points. The integral I2​(𝐪)I_{2}({\bf q}) reduces to the integral I1​(𝐪)I_{1}({\bf q}) by performing the summation over the unoccupied bands j′j^{\prime}.

For metallic systems a significantly larger number of 𝐤{\bf k}-points (Nk)(N_{k}) is necessary when the matrix elements as well as the energy denominator ϵ𝐤​j−ϵ𝐤±𝐪​j′\epsilon_{{\bf k}j}-\epsilon_{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}} are interpolated linearly within the tetrahedron. For these systems there are two sources of errors: the first is connected with the interpolation of the matrix elements and the second is connected with the interpolation of the Fermi surface. The latter can easily be circumvented in the linear–response calculation, since the Fermi surface can be determined accurately from the band structure of the unperturbed crystal. For the integrals I1​(𝐪)I_{1}({\bf q}) this can be done using the method described in Ref. 36 which is based on considering two, coarse and dense, meshes. In the tetrahedron method the integration weight of a particular 𝐤{\bf k}–point is calculated by integrating over the occupied parts of those tetrahedra that contain this point. The occupied part of the tetrahedron is found by linear interpolation between the energies at the corners of this tetrahedron. Suppose we introduce a much denser mesh that also contains the original coarse mesh. We will need only the energies ϵ𝐤​j\epsilon_{{\bf k}j} at this dense mesh, which will define the accurate Fermi surface (for example also by linear interpolation). Then, the occupied part of the tetrahedron at the coarse grid can be found by not interpolating linearly the energies known at its corners but as a piece of the accurate Fermi surface found with help of the dense grid. The same is applicable to the integrals I2​(𝐪):I_{2}({\bf q}): we consider the dense and the coarse grids. The band energies are known at the dense grid. To find the integration weights we must find a region in the tetrahedron where the state |𝐤​j⟩|{\bf k}j\rangle is occupied and the state |𝐤±𝐪​j⟩|{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j\rangle is unoccupied. This can be done using the linear interpolation but on the dense grid. We must also include the energy denominator ϵ𝐤​j−ϵ𝐤±𝐪​j′\epsilon_{{\bf k}j}-\epsilon_{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}}. This is also interpolated linearly but again using the dense grid. Consequently, all the effects from the energy bands and the Fermi surface are treated exactly in such scheme which allows us to avoid this source of errors in the integration.

Another source of errors is connected with the linear interpolation of the matrix elements. We have already mentioned that the matrix elements are normally smooth functions of wave vectors and one can expect that after eliminating the errors connected with the approximate treatment of the Fermi surface, the number of 𝐤{\bf k}–points need not be too large. However, in practical calculations a large cancellation occurs between the two kinds of the integrals, (42) and (43). If one uses different integration weights, it will lead to large numerical errors connected with the different convergency with respect to NkN_{k} in these integrals. Our task is thus to extract a large contribution from the integral of the type I2​(𝐪)I_{2}({\bf q}) and reduce it to the form I1​(𝐪).I_{1}({\bf q}). This is achieved by rewriting the energy denominator Δ=ϵ𝐤​j−ϵ𝐤±𝐪​j′\Delta=\epsilon_{{\bf k}j}-\epsilon_{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}} in the expression (43) as follows:

1Δ=ΔΔ2+δ2+1Δ​(1−Δ2Δ2+δ2),\frac{1}{\Delta}=\frac{\Delta}{\Delta^{2}+\delta^{2}}+\frac{1}{\Delta}\left(1-\frac{\Delta^{2}}{\Delta^{2}+\delta^{2}}\right), (44)

where the broadening δ\delta is usually chosen ∼0.1​R​y.\sim 0.1Ry. Then, the sum over unoccupied bands j′j^{\prime} in the integral containing Δ/(Δ2+δ2)\Delta/(\Delta^{2}+\delta^{2}) is readily performed because this expression remains regular when Δ→0.\Delta\rightarrow 0. Consequently, this integral is reduced to the integral of the type I1​(𝐪).I_{1}({\bf q}). The second integral in (44) contains 1/Δ1/\Delta and must be treated as the integral of the type I2​(𝐪)I_{2}({\bf q}) where the original matrix element M𝐤±𝐪​j′​𝐤​jM^{{\bf k}\pm{\bf q}j^{\prime}{\bf k}j} is now multiplied by the expression in brackets in (44). However, because the latter rapidly goes to zero for Δ≫δ\Delta\gg\delta, the whole integral remains small and it is non zero only for the band transitions j→j′j\rightarrow j^{\prime} between the states near the Fermi level. In practical calculations of the dynamical matrix, this procedure allows us to avoid the errors connecting with the large cancellations.

We finally mention that a simple correction formula which significantly improves the convergency of the integrals I1​(𝐪)I_{1}({\bf q}) by taking into account the curvature of the matrix elements beyond the linear interpolation was derived by Blöchl[32, 36]. Unfortunately, it is hard to derive such a correction for the integrals I2​(𝐪)I_{2}({\bf q}) because of the appearance of the energy denominator but we always use the Blöchl correction for the integrals (42).

d. Self-consistency at long wavelengths.

The change in the charge density (5) induced by the displacements of nuclei screens the external perturbation (4), and the linear–response equations (6)–(8) must, therefore, be solved self–consistently. Let us assume that we have found the response of the electrons, δ​ρ(0),\delta\rho^{(0)}, to the external perturbation δVext \delta V_{ext\text{ }}or the perturbation screened by some guessed δ​ρg​u​e​s​s\delta\rho^{guess} (here we omit ”±\pm” for simplicity). The latter could, for instance, be the rigid shifts of the charge density around the displaced nuclei and in practical calculations the external perturbation is always considered as the change in the bare Coulomb potential (4) plus the term ∇ρ\nabla\rho within the MT sphere. The response δ​ρ(0)\delta\rho^{(0)} is found along the lines described above and, consequently, it can be considered as some polarization operator Π^\hat{\Pi} that acts on δVext ,\delta V_{ext\text{ }},\,i.e.

δρ(0)=Π^δVext .\delta\rho^{(0)}=\hat{\Pi}\delta V_{ext\text{ }}. (45)

If we omit the terms containing the change in the basis functions and forget about the completeness problem of the unperturbed states, the operator Π^\hat{\Pi} is given by the independent–particle polarizability function π^\hat{\pi}:

π𝐪​(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle\pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= ∑𝐤​j​j′f𝐤​j−f𝐤+𝐪​j′ϵ𝐤​j−ϵ𝐤+𝐪​j′\displaystyle\sum_{{\bf k}jj^{\prime}}\frac{f_{{\bf k}j}-f_{{\bf k}+{\bf q}j^{\prime}}}{\epsilon_{{\bf k}j}-\epsilon_{{\bf k}+{\bf q}j^{\prime}}} (46)
×ψ𝐤+𝐪​j′​(𝐫)​ψ𝐤​j∗​(𝐫)​ψ𝐤+𝐪​j′∗​(𝐫′)​ψ𝐤​j​(𝐫′).\displaystyle\times\psi_{{\bf k}+{\bf q}j^{\prime}}({\bf r})\psi_{{\bf k}j}^{*}({\bf r})\psi_{{\bf k}+{\bf q}j^{\prime}}^{*}({\bf r}^{\prime})\psi_{{\bf k}j}({\bf r}^{\prime}).

The operator π\pi is an integral operator while Π^\hat{\Pi}\, is not necessarily one. It denotes the procedure how to construct the change δ​ρ\delta\rho from δVext .\delta V_{ext\text{ }}. In particular, Π^\hat{\Pi} contains those part of the operator π\pi in which the sum over conduction states runs only over the number which is equal to the number of the basis functions, Nb​a​s​i​s.N_{basis}. It also contains the contribution from the change in the basis functions according to (28), (36).

After the initial response δ​ρ(0)\delta\rho^{(0)} has been found, we have to calculate the screened perturbation (7). Let us call the Coulomb interaction, e2/|𝐫−𝐫′|,e^{2}/|{\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}|, for vCv_{C} and the exchange–correlation interaction in the LDA, d​Vx​c/d​ρ×δ⁡(𝐫−𝐫′),dV_{xc}/d\rho\times\delta({\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime}), for vx​c.v_{xc}. Then, the change δ​Ve​f​f\delta V_{eff} can be written as follows:

δ​Ve​f​f=δ​Ve​x​t+(vC+vx​c)​δ​ρ,\delta V_{eff}=\delta V_{ext}+(v_{C}+v_{xc})\delta\rho, (47)

and the new electronic response δ​ρ=Π^​δ​Ve​f​f.\delta\rho=\hat{\Pi}\delta V_{eff}.\, We thus see that the self-consistency of the induced charge density means solving the Dyson equation:

δ​ρ=δ​ρ(0)+Π^​(vC+vx​c)​δ​ρ.\delta\rho=\delta\rho^{(0)}+\hat{\Pi}(v_{C}+v_{xc})\delta\rho. (48)

When q→0,q\rightarrow 0, the integral vC​δ​ρv_{C}\delta\rho diverges as 1/q21/q^{2} which immediately means that searching for the solution of Eq. (48) by iterations, i.e. δ​ρ=δ​ρ(0)+Π^​(vC+vx​c)​δ​ρ(0)+…,\delta\rho=\delta\rho^{(0)}+\hat{\Pi}(v_{C}+v_{xc})\delta\rho^{(0)}+..., is impossible. However, it is possible when the input to the next, (OPENi+1)i+1)th, iteration is prepared by mixing the output and input densities from the previous, (i)(i)th, iteration, i.e. δ​ρi+1i​n​p=λm​i​x​δ​ρio​u​t+(1−λm​i​x)​δ​ρii​n​p,\delta\rho_{i+1}^{inp}=\lambda_{mix}\delta\rho_{i}^{out}+(1-\lambda_{mix})\delta\rho_{i}^{inp}, but the mixing parameter λm​i​x\lambda_{mix} must be chosen to be proportional to q2.q^{2}. This makes the standard mixing schemes in the long-wavelength limit extremely time–consuming.

This divergency problem is well known, and in the dielectric–matrix approach it is avoided by writing the solution (48) in the form:

δ​ρ=ϵ−1​δ​ρ(0),\delta\rho=\epsilon^{-1}\delta\rho^{(0)}, (49)

where ϵ−1=(1−Π​vC−Π​vx​c)−1\epsilon^{-1}=(1-\Pi v_{C}-\Pi v_{xc})^{-1} is an inverse dielectric matrix of the crystal. [The relation (49) is usually written for the potentials δ​Ve​f​f\delta V_{eff} and δ​Ve​x​t\delta V_{ext} but in the present context it is more convenient to remain within the density language.] If for a metal Π​vC\Pi v_{C} is proportional to N⁡(ϵF)/q2N(\epsilon_{F})/q^{2}, where N⁡(ϵF)N(\epsilon_{F}) is the density of states at the Fermi energy ϵF\epsilon_{F}, then ϵ−1\epsilon^{-1} behaves as q2q^{2} when q→0q\rightarrow 0\,: this is the well–known long-wavelength behavior of the metallic dielectric function. What we actually do when solving (48) by iterations is trying to sum up 1−x+x2−…=1/(1+x)1-x+x^{2}-...=1/(1+x) for x>1.x>1.

In order to avoid this problem we use Thomas–Fermi–like screening theory. To explain the idea we assume that the change in charge density and the potential are expanded in plane waves,

δ​ρ​(𝐫)=∑Gδ​ρ​(𝐆)​ei⁡(𝐪+𝐆)​𝐫.\delta\rho({\bf r})=\sum_{G}\delta\rho({\bf G})e^{i({\bf q}+{\bf G}){\bf r}}. (50)

We divide the Coulomb interaction vCv_{C} into a long-range and a short-range parts, i.e vC=vCl​o​n​g+vCs​h​o​r​t,v_{C}=v_{C}^{long}+v_{C}^{short}, where vCl​o​n​g=4​π​e2/q2×e​x​p​[i​𝐪​(𝐫−𝐫′)].v_{C}^{long}=4\pi e^{2}/q^{2}\times exp[i{\bf q}({\bf r}-{\bf r}^{\prime})]. The exchange-correlation in LDA is always short ranged and can be treated together with vCs​h​o​r​tv_{C}^{short}, i.e. vCs​h​o​r​t+vx​c=ws​h​o​r​t.v_{C}^{short}+v_{xc}=w^{short}. The Dyson equation can then be written as follows:

δ​ρ​(𝐫)=δ​ρ(0)​(𝐫)+4​π​e2q2​δ​ρ​(0)​Π𝐪​(𝐫)+{Π^​ws​h​o​r​t​δ​ρ}​(𝐫),\delta\rho({\bf r})=\delta\rho^{(0)}({\bf r})+\frac{4\pi e^{2}}{q^{2}}\delta\rho(0)\Pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf r})+\{\hat{\Pi}w^{short}\delta\rho\}({\bf r}), (51)

where we have separated out the divergent contribution, δ​ρ​(0)≡δ​ρ​(𝐆=0),\delta\rho(0)\equiv\delta\rho({\bf G}=0), and where we have called the response of electrons to the perturbation given by a single plane wave e​x​p​(i​𝐪𝐫)exp(i{\bf qr}) for Π𝐪​(𝐫).\Pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf r}). It can be written as an integral over the unit cell Ωc\Omega_{c}:

Π𝐪​(𝐫)=∫Ωcπ𝐪​(𝐫,𝐫′)​ei​𝐪𝐫′​d​𝐫′.\Pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf r)=}\int_{\Omega_{c}}\pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})e^{i{\bf qr}^{\prime}}d{\bf r}^{\prime}. (52)

The 𝐆=0{\bf G}=0 part of Eq. (51) can be written as follows:

δ​ρ​(0)=ϵl​o​n​g−1​(δ​ρ(0)​(0)+{Π^​ws​h​o​r​t​δ​ρ}​(𝐆=0)),\delta\rho(0)=\epsilon_{long}^{-1}\left(\delta\rho^{(0)}(0)+\{\hat{\Pi}w^{short}\delta\rho\}({\bf G}=0)\right), (53)

where we have introduced an effective dielectric constant:

ϵl​o​n​g=1−4​π​e2q2​Π𝐪​(𝐆=0).\epsilon_{long}=1-\frac{4\pi e^{2}}{q^{2}}\Pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf G}=0). (54)

Inserting Eq. (53) in to the Dyson equation (51) we obtain:

δ​ρ​(𝐫)=δ​ρ(0)​(𝐫)+4​π​e2q2+κD2\displaystyle\delta\rho({\bf r})=\delta\rho^{(0)}({\bf r})+\frac{4\pi e^{2}}{q^{2}+\kappa_{D}^{2}}
×(δ​ρ(0)​(0)+{Π^​ws​h​o​r​t​δ​ρ}​(𝐆=0))\displaystyle\times\left(\delta\rho^{(0)}(0)+\{\hat{\Pi}w^{short}\delta\rho\}({\bf G}=0)\right)
×Π𝐪​(𝐫)+{Π^​ws​h​o​r​t​δ​ρ}​(𝐫),\displaystyle\times\Pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf r})+\{\hat{\Pi}w^{short}\delta\rho\}({\bf r}), (55)

where κD2=−4​π​e2​Π𝐪​(𝐆=0)\kappa_{D}^{2}=-4\pi e^{2}\Pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf G}=0) is the Debye screening radius. The screened Dyson equation (55) is free of the difficulties discussed above and can be solved iteratively. First, one has to find the function Π𝐪​(𝐫)\Pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf r}) as the response of electrons to a single plane wave e​x​p​(i​𝐪𝐫),exp(i{\bf qr}), and from that obtain κD2.\kappa_{D}^{2}. Then the initial distribution δ​ρ(0)​(𝐫)\delta\rho^{(0)}({\bf r}) is calculated. During the iterations one first finds the response to the short–range part of the perturbation, i.e. {Π^​ws​h​o​r​t​δ​ρ}​(𝐫)\{\hat{\Pi}w^{short}\delta\rho\}({\bf r}), and, secondly, the long-wavelength contribution is added as given by the second term in the right–hand side of Eq. (55). The output change in the charge density is usually mixed with the input δ​ρ\delta\rho to obtain an input for the new iteration. This makes the self–consistent cycle stable, but the mixing parameter λm​i​x\lambda_{mix}\,in this case does not have to go to zero for 𝐪→0{\bf q}\rightarrow 0\, and it is usually chosen to be 0.2−0.5.0.2-0.5. In practical applications we have found that the number of iterations required to solve (55) is about 1010 while for solving the original Dyson equation (48) the number of iterations varies from 5050 to 200200 depending on the length |𝐪||{\bf q|} of the wave vector . The latter is, of course, not true for those phonon modes where δ​ρ​(0)≡0\delta\rho(0)\equiv 0 by symmetry.

One can obviously consider the screening of not only the component δ​V​(𝐆)∼δ​ρ​(𝐆)/|𝐪+𝐆|2\delta V({\bf G})\sim\delta\rho({\bf G})/|{\bf q}+{\bf G}|^{2} with 𝐆=0{\bf G}=0 but all the components within a certain sphere |𝐪+𝐆|≤Gc​u​t​o​f​f.|{\bf q}+{\bf G}|\leq G_{cutoff}. This, for instance, is necessary for those zone–boundary wave vectors where |𝐪|=|𝐪+𝐆|.|{\bf q}|=|{\bf q}+{\bf G}|.\,In this case the function Π𝐪​(𝐫)\Pi_{{\bf q}}({\bf r}) is replaced by the functions Π𝐪+𝐆​(𝐫)\Pi_{{\bf q}+{\bf G}}({\bf r}), i.e. at the beginning it is necessary to calculate the response of the electrons to the perturbation e​x​p​[i⁡(𝐪+𝐆)​𝐫]exp[i({\bf q}+{\bf G}){\bf r}]. The corresponding Dyson equation should be written again to account for the fact that ϵl​o​n​g\epsilon_{long} is now the matrix ϵl​o​n​g​(𝐪+𝐆,𝐪+𝐆′).\epsilon_{long}({\bf q}+{\bf G},{\bf q}+{\bf G}^{\prime}). This will reduce the number of iterations even more.

Finally, we would like to point out that it should be possible to apply the same idea to the self–consistency problem in the standard band structure calculation. In the crystal, due to electroneutrality of the charge density, ρ⁡(𝐆=0)=0.\rho({\bf G}=0)=0. However, for those reciprocal–lattice vectors which are small, the components of the potential V⁡(𝐆)∼ρ⁡(𝐆)/|𝐆|2V({\bf G})\sim\rho({\bf G})/|{\bf G}|^{2} might be large. This is especially the case for large many–atomic unit cells. As a consequence, the mixing parameter λm​i​x\lambda_{mix}\, has to be chosen very small. The procedure described above will require the calculation of the polarizability (46) with 𝐪=0{\bf q}=0\, at each self–consistent iteration, i.e. the response of electrons to the plane waves e​x​p​[i​𝐆𝐫]exp[i{\bf Gr}] according to the expression (52) for all small vectors || 𝐆|≤Gc​u​t​o​f​f.{\bf G|}\leq G_{cutoff}. The cutoff can be chosen as the radius of the smallest first coordination sphere in GG–space. The computational time for finding the ΠG​(𝐫)\Pi_{G}({\bf r})–functions should presumably not exceed the time of one self–consistent iteration while the total number of iterations needed to reach the convergency is expected to decrease by approximately one order of magnitude, which is the case in linear–response calculation. Note that the idea just outlined is different from the idea of finding the self–consistent charge transfer in terms of the linear–response theory [38]. For large cells we are screening the small GG–components of the potential which result from some average density distribution. On the other hand, such details as the charge transfer between nearest atoms is described by large GG–components of ρ⁡(𝐆).\rho({\bf G}).

IV. APPLICATIONS.

In recent publications[11, 13, 14] we have demonstrated the ability of our linear–response method to compute whole phonon dispersions and electron–phonon interactions in such complicated systems as transition metals N​bNb and M​oMo. In the present paper we will describe application of the method for calculating phonon dispersions in the materials with a few atoms per unit cell and with a relatively open crystalline structures. Two systems have been chosen for the applications. The first one is S​iSi which is an excellent test case because of its open diamond structure. The second one is a transition–metal carbide N​b​CNbC. This is a well–known classic superconductor with Tc=11.5​KT_{c}=11.5K and its phonon dispersions show many anomalies that are not present in other simple–metallic and insulating systems. Studying these anomalies as well as their influence on superconductivity and transport is interesting in itself and also represents a hard test for our method. Here we will only describe the calculations for the phonon dispersion curves in N​b​CNbC and compare the results with experiments. The calculated electron–phonon interaction and transport properties will be published elsewhere.

a. Si.

S​iSi is a well studied elemental semiconductor from both experimental and theoretical sides and its phonon dispersions have been measured long time ago[39]. Recent linear–response[6, 9] and supercell[17] calculations have allowed to determine its lattice dynamics for the wave vectors in the entire Brillouin zone and the results show a good agreement with the experiment. These calculations were based on the linear–augmented–plane–wave and plane-wave pseudopotential methods. Within the localized–orbital representation employed in the LMTO method it is generally difficult to treat the materials with the diamond structure and, to reach close packing, interstitial spheres are usually placed into the empty sites of the lattice. This complicates the determination of the dynamical matrix. However, this problem is avoided in our method by the use of the Fourier transform for the LMTOs in the interstitial region.

We calculate the dynamical matrix of S​iSi as a function of wave vector for a set of irreducible 𝐪{\bf q}-points in a (6,6,6)(6,6,6)–reciprocal lattice grid (16 points per 1/481/48th part of the BZ). The (I,J,K)(I,J,K) reciprocal lattice (or Monkhorst–Pack) grid is defined in a usual manner: 𝐪i​j​k=iI​𝐆1+jJ​𝐆2+kK​𝐆3{\bf q}_{ijk}=\frac{i}{I}{\bf G}_{1}+\frac{j}{J}{\bf G}_{2}+\frac{k}{K}{\bf G}_{3}, where 𝐆1,𝐆2,𝐆3{\bf G}_{1},{\bf G}_{2},{\bf G}_{3} are the primitive translations in reciprocal space. The details of the calculations for every 𝐪{\bf q}–point are the following: We use 3​κ−s​p​d3\kappa-spd LMTO basis set (27 orbitals per atom) with the one-center expansions inside the MT-spheres performed up to lm​a​x=6.l_{max}=6. In the interstitial region, the ss, pp and dd – basis functions are expanded in plane waves up to 15.1, 22.3, 31.7 Ry (282, 530, 868 plane waves) respectively. The induced charge densities and screened potentials are represented inside the MT–spheres by spherical harmonics up to lm​a​x=6l_{max}=6 and by plane waves with the 110.2 Ry energy cutoff (5208 plane waves) in the interstitial region. The 𝐤{\bf k}–integration over the BZ is performed over the (6,6,6)(6,6,6) – grid (the same grid as for the phonon wave vectors 𝐪{\bf q}) by means of the improved tetrahedron method[36] which is identical in the case of S​iSi to the special–point method of Monkhorst and Pack. The MT–sphere radius was taken to be 2.214 a.u. and the Barth–Hedin–like exchange–correlation formulae after Ref. 40 are employed. We use theoretically determined lattice parameter in the calculation (the volume ratio V/Ve​x​p=0.991V/V_{exp}=0.991).

Fig.1 shows a comparison between calculated and experimental phonon dispersion curves along the major high–symmetry directions. The calculated phonon density of states is plotted at the right part in the figure. The theoretical frequencies are denoted by circles and the experimental ones are denoted by triangles. The lines result from the interpolation between the theoretical points. The calculated and experimental phonon frequencies at the high-symmetry points Γ\Gamma, X,X, and LL\, are also listed in Table 1. We see that the agreement between theory and experiment is very good. Especially, in the optical region the discrepancy is about 1-1.5%, which is surprising because the accuracy of the measured phonon modes is of the same order of magnitude. We also reproduce the extended flat regions of the transverse acoustic modes indicating the accurate description of long–range interactions between S​iSi -atoms as well as the correct long-wavelength behavior showing the good accuracy of calculated elastic properties of this crystal. Larger discrepancy is found for the frequencies of the TA modes, where the theoretical branches are approximately 10% softer than the experimental ones. For instance, the calculated frequency of the XT​AX_{TA} – mode is 4.00 THz while ωe​x​p​(XT​A)=4.49±0.06\omega_{exp}(X_{TA})=4.49\pm 0.06 THz[39]. The same kind of discrepancy has also been recently reported in Refs. 9, 17. The agreement is slightly improved when we recalculate the dynamical matrix at the XX – point using the experimental lattice constant. We have found that the frequency of the XT​AX_{TA} – mode is increased from 4.00 to 4.27 THz. This shows that the mode has a large negative Gruneizen parameter and it is thus very sensitive to the unit–cell volume used in the calculation. Because of the large LMTO basis sets, large lm​a​xl\,_{max} and plane–wave energy cutoffs this discrepancy is hard to relate to the internal parameters in the calculation and it is most likely connected with the local density approximation.

b. NbC.

The lattice dynamical properties of transition-metal carbides and, especially, N​b​CNbC have attracted much attention in the past because of the existence of pronounced anomalies in its acoustic branches and their influence to superconductivity . While some model calculations of the phonon dispersions exist in the literature and various mechanisms explaining these anomalies have been proposed[41], no ab initio investigation of the lattice dynamics for N​b​CNbC have so far been performed. Here we apply the linear–response approach to the phonon spectrum of N​b​CNbC\, in order to check the accuracy of our method.

The dynamical matrix of N​b​CNbC\, is calculated at the 2929 irreducible 𝐪{\bf q} – points of a (8,8,8)(8,8,8) reciprocal–lattice grid. The self–consistent calculations performed for every wave vector involve the following parameters: 3​κ−s​p​d3\kappa-spd LMTO basis per N​bNb atom (27 orbitals) and 3​κ−s​p3\kappa-sp LMTO basis per carbon atom (12 orbitals). The one–center expansions inside the MT–spheres are performed up to lm​a​x=6.l_{max}=6. In the interstitial region the basis functions are expanded in plane waves up to 13.4, 19.6, 26.9 Ry (136, 228, 338 plane waves) for, respectively, s,ps,p and dd – orbitals of N​bNb, and up to 24.1, 35.8 Ry (306, 536 plane waves) for s,ps,p –orbitals of C.C. The changes in the charge densities and the potentials are represented inside the MT–spheres by spherical harmonics up to lm​a​x=6l_{max}=6 and by plane waves with an 121 Ry energy cutoff (3382 plane waves) in the interstitial region. The 𝐤{\bf k}–space integration for the matrix elements is performed over a (8,8,8)(8,8,8) – grid (the same grid as for the phonon wave vectors 𝐪{\bf q}) by means of the improved tetrahedron method[36]. However, the integration weights for the 𝐤{\bf k}–points of this grid have been found to take into account the effects arising from the Fermi surface and the energy bands precisely. This is done with help of a (32,32,32)(32,32,32) grid (897 𝐤{\bf k} – points per 1/481/48 BZ) as we explained in Section III(c) of this paper. The MT–sphere radius of N​bNb is taken to be 2.411 a.u. and the radius of the carbon sphere is 1.786 a.u. The Barth–Hedin–like exchange–correlation formulae after Ref. 40 are employed. As in the case of S​iSi, we also use the theoretically determined lattice parameter in this calculation (the volume ratio V/Ve​x​p=0.982V/V_{exp}=0.982).

The results of our calculations are presented in Fig. 2, where we compare theoretically determined phonon dispersions (circles) with those measured by inelastic–neutron–scattering technique [42] (triangles). The calculated phonon density of states is plotted at the right part of the figure. The lines are simply the result of interpolation between the theoretical points. Since the 𝐪−{\bf q}- grid (8,8,8)(8,8,8) considered here is still too coarse to resolve the anomaly of the longitudinal acoustic branch near the wave vector (0.6,0,0)​ 2​π/a(0.6,0,0)\,2\pi/a\,, we have performed a separate calculation for the 𝐪{\bf q} –point (0.625,0,0)(0.625,0,0) which fits to the (16,16,16)(16,16,16) – grid in 𝐤{\bf k}–space. We see that the agreement between theory and experiment is good. Most of the calculated frequencies agree within a few percent with those measured despite of the fact that we have used only 29 𝐤{\bf k}–points for the BZ–integration. (We list for comparison our calculated and experimental phonon frequencies at the high–symmetry points Γ\Gamma, X,X, and LL\, in Table 2.) The theory reproduces the major anomalies presented in the acoustic branches: the well-known anomaly near the wave vector (0.6,0,0)​ 2​π/a(0.6,0,0)\,2\pi/a which is also present and well described[11] within our linear–response method in pure N​bNb crystal; the anomaly of the longitudinal mode near the wave vector (0.5,0.5,0)​ 2​π/a(0.5,0.5,0)\,2\pi/a as well as large softening of both TA and LA modes near the LL –point. Moreover, we also predict an anomalous behavior of the lowest transverse acoustic mode along the (ξ​ξ​0)(\xi\xi 0) direction near the wave vector (0.5,0.5,0)​ 2​π/a(0.5,0.5,0)\,2\pi/a .Here the frequencies are not known experimentally. The anomaly found by us is, however, less pronounced compared to the results of double–shell model calculations of Weber [43] while we have certainly not too many points along this direction to judge about its exact dispersion.

V. CONCLUSION.

In conclusion, we have described in detail an all–electron linear–response approach based on density functional theory and the LMTO technique. The method is developed to calculate lattice dynamical properties of crystalline solids and is uniquely applicable for the systems with broad and narrow energy bands. For test purposes, we have applied the method to compute phonon dispersions for S​iSi and N​b​CNbC which have open structures and two atoms per unit cell. The results of our applications are in a good agreement with the experiment. We have thus shown that accurate calculations of lattice dynamics are now possible even for such complicated systems as transition–metal compounds. In the forthcoming paper[44] we give a description of our method for calculating electron–phonon interactions and apply the method to compute lattice–dynamical, superconducting and transport properties for a large number of elemental metals (a brief report of this work has appeared already[13]). In another publication [45] we describe an application of the method for computing electron–phonon–coupling strength in C​a−S​r−C​u−OCa-Sr-Cu-O high-TcT_{c} superconductor.

APPENDIX: Fourier transform of pseudoLMTOs.

Consider a Hankel function Kκ​L​(𝐫)=Kκ​l​(r)​il​Yl​m​(𝐫)K_{\kappa L}({\bf r})=K_{\kappa l}(r)i^{l}Y_{lm}({\bf r}) of energy κ2\kappa^{2} which is singular at the origin. The three–dimensional Fourier transform of this function Kκ​L​(𝐤)K_{\kappa L}({\bf k}) is known to behave as kl−2k^{l-2} for large k.k.\,The task is to substitute the divergent part of Kκ​l​(r)K_{\kappa l}(r)\, inside some sphere ss by a smooth regular but otherwise arbitrary function. This function is chosen so that the Fourier transform is convergent fast. In the full–potential LMTO method of Ref. 29, the augmenting function is the linear combination of the Bessel function Jκ​LJ_{\kappa L} and its energy derivative J˙κ​L\dot{J}_{\kappa L} matched together with its first–order radial derivative with the Hankel function at the sphere boundary. The Fourier transform becomes convergent as k−4k^{-4}. One can obviously include higher–order energy derivatives J(n)κ​L\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(n)}}{{J}}_{\kappa L} in order to have a smooth matching at the sphere up to the order nn. This was done in connection with the problem of solving the Poisson equation in Ref. 34. The Fourier transform here converges as k−(3+n)k^{-(3+n)} but the prefactor increases as (2​l+2​n+3)!!(2l+2n+3)!! and this prohibits the use of large values of nn. A similar procedure has been also used in the LMTO method of Ref. 30. In the present work we will use a different approach based on the Ewald method. Instead of substituting the divergent part only for r<sr<s we consider the solution of the equation:

(−∇2−κ2)​K~κ​L​(𝐫)=al​(rs)l​e−r2​η2+κ2/η2​il​Yl​m​(𝐫),(-\nabla^{2}-\kappa^{2})\tilde{K}_{\kappa L}({\bf r})=a_{l}\left(\frac{r}{s}\right)^{l}e^{-r^{2}\eta^{2}+\kappa^{2}/\eta^{2}}i^{l}Y_{lm}({\bf r}), (56)

The function on the right-hand side of the Helmholtz equation is a decaying Gaussian. The parameter ala_{l} is a normalization constant: al=2/π​(2​η2)l+3/2​s2​l+1/(2​l−1)!!a_{l}=\sqrt{2/\pi}(2\eta^{2})^{l+3/2}s^{2l+1}/(2l-1)!!. The most important parameter is η\eta. It is chosen such that the Gaussian is approximately zero when r>sr>s and η\eta must depend on ll as well as the sphere radius s.s. The solution K~κ​L​(𝐫)\tilde{K}_{\kappa L}({\bf r}) is thus the Hankel function for large rr, it is a regular function for small rr and it is smooth together with its radial derivatives at any rr. The function K~κ​l​(r)\tilde{K}_{\kappa l}(r) can be calculated in terms of the following error-function-like contour integral:

K~κ​l​(r)=(2​s)l+1π​(2​l−1)!!​rl​∫0+ηξ2​l​e−r2​ξ2+κ2/4​ξ2​𝑑ξ.\tilde{K}_{\kappa l}(r)=\frac{(2s)^{l+1}}{\sqrt{\pi}(2l-1)!!}r^{l}\int_{0+}^{\eta}\xi^{2l}e^{-r^{2}\xi^{2}+\kappa^{2}/4\xi^{2}}d\xi. (57)

When η→∞\eta\rightarrow\infty this integral is known as the Hankel integral. The most important result is that the Fourier transform of K~κ​l​(r)\tilde{K}_{\kappa l}(r) decays exponentially. It is given by:

K~κ​l​(r)=2π​sl+1(2​l−1)!!​∫0∞k2​𝑑k​jl​(k​r)​kl​e(κ2−k2)/4​η2k2−κ2.\tilde{K}_{\kappa l}(r)=\frac{2}{\pi}\frac{s^{l+1}}{(2l-1)!!}\int_{0}^{\infty}k^{2}dkj_{l}(kr)\frac{k^{l}e^{(\kappa^{2}-k^{2})/4\eta^{2}}}{k^{2}-\kappa^{2}}. (58)

Restoring the original notations, the pseudoLMTOs χ~κ​R​L𝐤​(𝐫)\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}^{{\bf k}}({\bf r}) are the Bloch waves of wave vector 𝐤{\bf k} as defined in Eq. (27). The Fourier coefficients χ~κ​R​L​(𝐤+𝐆)\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}({\bf k}+{\bf G}) are given by:

χ~κ​R​L(𝐤+𝐆)=4​πΩcsRl+1(2​l−1)!!|𝐤+𝐆|l|𝐤+𝐆|2−κ2×\displaystyle\tilde{\chi}_{\kappa RL}({\bf k}+{\bf G})=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega_{c}}\frac{s_{R}^{l+1}}{(2l-1)!!}\frac{|{\bf k}+{\bf G}|^{l}}{|{\bf k}+{\bf G}|^{2}-\kappa^{2}}\times
e(κ2−|𝐤+𝐆|2)/4​ηR​l2​YL​(𝐤+𝐆)​e−i⁡(𝐤+𝐆)​𝐑,\displaystyle e^{(\kappa^{2}-|{\bf k}+{\bf G}|^{2})/4\eta_{Rl}^{2}}Y_{L}({\bf k}+{\bf G})e^{-i({\bf k}+{\bf G}){\bf R}}, (59)

where Ωc\Omega_{c} is the volume of the unit cell and where we have subscripted η\eta with the indexes R​lRl and ss with R.R.

In practical calculations the parameter ηR​l\eta_{Rl} can be chosen from the ratio between the Hankel function at the sphere and the solution of Eq. (56), i.e. K~κ​l​(sR)/Kκ​l​(sR)=1+δ.\tilde{K}_{\kappa l}(s_{R})/K_{\kappa l}(s_{R})=1+\delta. The error |δ||\delta| is usually taken not larger than 0.030.03 which leads to the number of plane waves per atom needed for the convergency in (27) varying from 150 to 250 when l=2.l=2. For the s,p−s,p-orbitals this number is smaller by a factor of 2−3.2-3.
